title: Should Meridian Automate the First Inspection?
description: Paired workplace arguments about whether a promising automation pilot justifies expansion and staffing changes.
subject: rla
author: Chee Skool
reviewNotes: Mixed-source Arguments practice reviewed for source comparison, evidence quality, one-best-answer logic, and ER transfer.

questions.prompt: Which argument is better supported for the claim that the camera system is ready for permanent staffing reductions?

options.text: Source A, because a lower scan time automatically means fewer inspectors are needed.
options.whyWrong: The proposal itself calls for more testing before permanent staffing changes and does not measure the full work inspectors perform.

options.text: Source B, because it identifies unmeasured conditions and support costs that matter before using the pilot to justify permanent staffing changes.
Source A, because 116 correct flags prove the system never misses important defects.
options.whyWrong: The pilot confirmed five visible defects were missed.

options.text: Source B, because any automated tool that makes one error must be rejected.
options.whyWrong: Grant raises legitimate limits, but an absolute no-error standard would not by itself be a sound comparison.

explanation.whyCorrect: For permanent staffing changes, the one-line pilot leaves major questions about generalization, support time, and tasks the camera cannot perform.
explanation.quickTip: Match the strength of the evidence to the size and permanence of the decision.

questions.prompt: What is Nordin's strongest response to Grant's focus on the five missed defects?

options.text: Missed defects do not matter if scan time is lower.
options.whyWrong: Nordin does not dismiss misses; she proposes comparing complete systems and measuring them.

options.text: The camera should replace all inspectors because humans also make errors.
options.whyWrong: Her proposal keeps humans in verification and harder cases.

options.text: The relevant comparison is camera-assisted human inspection versus human-only inspection, because neither system should be assumed perfect.
The five misses were caused entirely by reflective packaging.
options.whyWrong: Reflective packaging is linked to false alerts, not all missed defects.

explanation.whyCorrect: Nordin reframes the standard from perfection to comparative system performance, which is the more useful decision question.
explanation.quickTip: Watch for arguments that compare a real system with an impossible perfect alternative.

questions.prompt: Which evidence gap do BOTH writers ultimately support addressing?

options.text: Whether the system works across a broader range of products and operating conditions.
Whether every inspector prefers camera technology.
options.whyWrong: Neither writer makes employee preference the central missing evidence.

options.text: Whether the company can eliminate all mechanical checks.
options.whyWrong: Both recognize tasks the camera cannot perform.

options.text: Whether the camera can be operated without electricity.

explanation.whyCorrect: Both proposals call for further testing beyond the narrow one-line conditions, though they differ on how that test should be designed.
explanation.quickTip: Shared evidence needs can exist even when writers disagree about readiness.

questions.prompt: Why is the 19-second figure not sufficient by itself to establish total labor savings?

options.text: The figure measures only first-scan and flagged-image review time and may exclude engineering support, unusual false-alert handling, and other inspection tasks.
Any time measurement is unreliable if it is below one minute.
options.whyWrong: Duration does not determine whether a measurement is valid.

options.text: The pilot used 4,200 assemblies, which is too many to analyze.
options.whyWrong: A larger sample is not inherently a weakness.

options.text: The system found visible defects rather than mechanical defects.
options.whyWrong: That limitation matters to system scope, but the specific labor-savings gap is omitted work and support time.

explanation.whyCorrect: A partial process-time measure cannot automatically be treated as the net labor cost of the full inspection system.
explanation.quickTip: Ask what work the number includes and what work it leaves outside the measurement.

questions.prompt: Which next study would best resolve the central disagreement?

options.text: Ask customers whether they think cameras look modern.
options.whyWrong: Appearance preference does not compare inspection quality or cost.

options.text: Repeat the exact same six-week conditions without changing any measurement.
options.whyWrong: This would add volume but not address new product/lighting conditions or full-system costs.

options.text: Compare human-only and camera-assisted inspection across multiple product lines and varied conditions, tracking misses, false alerts, total labor/support time, and mechanical-check outcomes.
Buy the system permanently and infer its value from whether managers like it.
options.whyWrong: Permanent adoption before resolving the disputed outcomes would not create a controlled comparison.

explanation.whyCorrect: This design directly measures the quality, generalization, and total-work questions both writers raise.
explanation.quickTip: The best next evidence targets the decisive disagreement rather than collecting more of the same narrow data.

questions.prompt: Which summary most fairly represents both positions?

options.text: Nordin says the camera is perfect; Grant says cameras never work.
options.whyWrong: Neither source takes such an absolute position.

options.text: Nordin sees the pilot as promising evidence for camera-assisted inspection and broader testing; Grant argues that the current test is too narrow to justify expansion or staffing conclusions without tougher conditions and fuller cost measures.
Both writers agree inspectors should be removed immediately.
The only disagreement is whether reflective packaging should be banned.
options.whyWrong: Reflective packaging is one false-alert issue, not the main policy disagreement.

explanation.whyCorrect: This summary preserves the evidence, caution, and different thresholds for expansion without exaggerating either side.
explanation.quickTip: A fair synthesis states the strongest version of each argument.

curriculum.learningObjective: Evaluate claims, evidence, reasoning, and multiple sources under GED-style conditions.
